notes.big_picture: This course teaches you how to build agentic AI systems that go beyond simple single prompts by using iterative, multi-step workflows. You will learn the core design patterns of reflection, tool use, planning, and multi-agent collaboration to create autonomous applications. The curriculum emphasizes a practical, disciplined development process starting from quick prototyping to rigorous evaluations and error analysis. By breaking down complex tasks and integrating external tools or code execution, you can dramatically improve LLM performance. Ultimately, these techniques allow you to design flexible, robust workflows for real-world automation tasks.

The four core design patterns are reflection, tool use, planning, and multi-agent collaboration.
Reflection lets an AI model review and improve its own outputs using external feedback.
Tool use allows LLMs to request function calls or code execution to gather information and take actions.
Model Context Protocol standardizes how applications connect to tools and data sources.
Building agentic AI requires a disciplined development cycle of prototyping, evaluations, and error analysis.
Component-level evaluations help isolate system noise and test individual agent changes faster.
Planning allows an LLM to write step-by-step instructions in formats like JSON or code to handle complex tasks.
Multi-agent workflows break down complex problems by assigning specific roles like researchers or writers to different AI entities.

notes.importance_reason: This lesson introduces the foundational concept of agentic AI workflows and contrasts them with single-prompt generation.
notes.tldr: Agentic AI workflows use an iterative, multi-step process to produce much better results than writing everything in a single prompt.
notes.summary: Standard AI usage involves prompting a large language model to generate text from start to finish in one go, much like writing without a backspace. In contrast, an agentic workflow breaks a task down into multiple steps, such as outlining, researching, drafting, and revising. This iterative process takes longer but results in a much higher quality work product. You will learn to decompose complex tasks into individual steps and build components to execute them. The course uses a practical research agent example to demonstrate these concepts across various industries.

key_ideas.detail: Asking an AI to write an entire essay in one go without backspace is linear and restrictive, though models still perform surprisingly well.

Both ends of the spectrum offer valuable applications, though highly autonomous agents are harder to control and remain an active area of research. lessons.title: Task decomposition: Identifying the steps in a workflow

notes.importance_reason: It teaches how to break down complex tasks into manageable steps for agentic workflows, which is fundamental to building AI agents.
notes.tldr: Task decomposition involves breaking complex processes into smaller steps that can be handled by LLMs, code, or tools, and then refining them iteratively.
notes.summary: When building agentic workflows, you start by looking at how a human would accomplish a task and breaking it down into discrete steps. Each step is evaluated to see if an LLM, short code, function call, or tool can perform it. If the initial results are not good enough, you can further decompose complex steps into finer sub-steps like drafting, reviewing, and revising. Available building blocks include large language models, specialized AI models, and software tools like APIs, databases, and code execution. Ultimately, building effective workflows is an iterative process of testing, decomposing further, and improving performance.

key_ideas.detail: Look at how a human would complete a task step-by-step to figure out how to structure the agentic workflow.
Ask whether each decomposed step can be successfully executed by an LLM, a short piece of code, or a software tool.
If a workflow produces poor or disjointed results, take complex steps and break them down further into sub-steps.
Workflows are built by sequencing large language models, specialized AI models, and software tools like APIs and databases.

notes.importance_reason: Disciplined evaluation processes are a core predictor of success when building agentic workflows.
notes.tldr: Build your agent first, discover its errors by reading outputs, and use objective code or an LLM judge to evaluate and improve it.
notes.summary: Building agentic workflows successfully requires a disciplined evaluation process known as evals. Because it is hard to anticipate what will go wrong in advance, the best practice is to build the system first, examine outputs manually for flaws, and then create metrics to track and fix those issues. You can use simple code to check for objective criteria, like counting unexpected competitor mentions. For more subjective traits, you can use another LLM as a judge to grade the quality of the output. Additionally, you can perform error analysis by reading through intermediate outputs or traces to find where the agent falls short.

key_ideas.detail: It is difficult to anticipate all potential problems in advance, so you should build the agent first and then examine its outputs to see what needs improvement.
When criteria are black and white, such as whether an agent mentioned a competitor by name, you can write simple code to calculate the error rate.
For more subjective outputs like essay quality, you can prompt another LLM to review the text and assign a score.
Reading through the intermediate outputs or traces of every single step helps you spot exact opportunities to improve the agentic workflow.

Use this eval score to track your progress as you update the prompt or system to eliminate competitor mentions.

lessons.title: Reflection to improve outputs of a task

notes.importance_reason: This lesson introduces the core concept of the reflection design pattern, which is a fundamental building block for agentic AI workflows.
notes.tldr: The reflection design pattern lets an AI model review and improve its own outputs, especially when aided by external feedback like error logs.
notes.summary: Just as humans review and fix their own writing, large language models can use a reflection process to improve their initial outputs. You can prompt a model to generate a first draft, and then prompt the same or a different model to review it and create an improved second draft. This approach works for tasks like writing emails or generating code. Reflection becomes significantly more powerful when you feed external information, such as execution error messages, back into the model during the review step. While reflection does not guarantee perfection, it provides a modest and useful performance boost.

key_ideas.detail: An AI model evaluates its own initial output (v1) and generates an improved second version (v2) using a separate prompt.
You can use different AI models for different tasks, such as using reasoning models specifically to check code for bugs.
Reflection is much more powerful when you feed outside information, like code execution errors, back into the review step.
The reflection design pattern is not magic and will not yield 100% perfection, but it gives a reliable performance bump.

notes.importance_reason: This lesson introduces the core comparison between direct generation and reflection workflows, which is fundamental to the course.

notes.summary: Direct generation asks an LLM to produce an answer in one go using zero-shot prompting. However, research shows that adding a reflection step consistently improves task performance across various models and applications. Reflection is especially helpful for complex structured data like nested JSON, step-by-step instructions, and creative tasks like checking domain names for unintended meanings. Writing effective reflection prompts involves asking the model to review a first draft against a clear set of specific criteria. By checking tone, factual accuracy, and formatting constraints, the model can produce a better second draft.

Prompting an LLM to perform a task without including any example input-output pairs in the prompt.

flashcards.q: What is zero-shot prompting?
flashcards.a: Prompting an LLM to generate an answer without providing any examples of desired outputs in the prompt.

flashcards.q: Why use a reflection workflow instead of direct generation?
flashcards.a: Research shows reflection improves task performance by allowing the model to spot errors, check constraints, and refine its output.

notes.importance_reason: It shows a practical application of the reflection pattern using a multimodal LLM to improve chart generation.
notes.tldr: Reflection using a multimodal LLM helps improve messy initial charts into clear visualizations.
notes.summary: In this lesson, you look at a coding workflow where an agent generates a chart from coffee sales data. The initial code often produces a poor visualization, such as a confusing stacked bar plot. By feeding both the code and the generated image into a multimodal LLM, the model can visually inspect the figure and critique it. The LLM then updates the code to create a clearer, better-formatted graph. You can also mix and match different models and use specific criteria to guide the reflection process.

key_ideas.detail: An LLM writes Python code to create a plot using data from a spreadsheet.
A multimodal LLM accepts both the generated code and the resulting image as inputs to critique the visualization.
Giving the reflection prompt specific criteria like readability and clarity helps the LLM figure out how to improve the plot.
You can use different models for the initial generation and the reflection step, such as using a reasoning model for reflection.

example.title: Improving Coffee Sales Plots
example.scenario: An agent generates a messy stacked bar plot comparing Q1 coffee sales across years using a spreadsheet CSV file.
steps: An LLM writes version 1 of the Python code to plot the spreadsheet data.
The code runs and outputs a poorly formatted stacked bar plot.
Version 1 code and the generated plot image are fed into a multimodal LLM.
The multimodal LLM critiques the image for visual clarity and updates the code.
The new code executes and produces a clean, separated bar graph.
example.takeaway: Multimodal reflection allows an agent to look at its own visual mistakes and fix the code to make a better chart.

watch.why: Shows the initial stacked bar plot generated by the first version of the code.
Shows the improved bar graph generated after the multimodal reflection step.

terms.definition: An LLM that can accept both text and image inputs to perform visual reasoning.
Comma-separated values used as a simple spreadsheet file format.

flashcards.q: Why is a multimodal model useful in the chart generation workflow?
flashcards.a: It can accept the generated plot image as input, inspect it visually, and critique how to make it better.

flashcards.q: What helps the LLM figure out how to improve the chart during reflection?
flashcards.a: Giving it specific criteria like readability, clarity, and completeness.

notes.importance_reason: This lesson teaches how to evaluate whether reflection workflows actually improve system performance using objective and subjective metrics.
notes.tldr: Use evals with ground-truth answers or rubric-based LLM judges to measure whether reflection improves your agent's performance.
notes.summary: Reflection can improve system outputs, but it also adds an extra step that slows down the system. To justify keeping reflection, developers build evaluations using a set of test prompts and compare outputs with and without reflection. For tasks with clear right or wrong answers, code-based evaluation against ground-truth data works best. For subjective tasks like image generation, using an LLM as a judge with binary rubric criteria provides more reliable results than direct pairwise comparisons.

key_ideas.detail: Reflection adds an extra step to your workflow, so you need evals to prove it actually improves output quality before committing to it.
When tasks have a clear right or wrong answer, you can collect a set of prompts with ground-truth answers and use code to measure accuracy percentage.
Comparing two subjective outputs directly using an LLM often fails due to position bias, where the model favors the first option presented.
Instead of open-ended comparisons, you can use an LLM to assess a single output against a set of binary criteria and sum the scores for consistent results.

example.title: Evaluating a SQL Generation Workflow
example.scenario: You want to know if adding a reflection step helps an LLM write better database queries for a retail store application.
steps: Collect 10 to 15 test prompts along with their correct ground-truth answers.
Run the workflow without reflection and record the percentage of correct answers fetched.
Run the workflow with a second reflection LLM improving the SQL query before execution.
Compare the success rates, such as 87 percent accuracy without reflection versus 95 percent with reflection.
Use these metrics to test and tune different prompt ideas for your reflection step.
example.takeaway: Building objective evals helps you systematically measure performance gains and choose the best prompts for your application.

The verified correct answer used to test whether an AI system's output is right or wrong.
Using a large language model to assess and score the quality of outputs generated by another system.
The tendency of an LLM to favor the first option presented to it when asked to compare choices.

flashcards.q: Why is it important to evaluate reflection workflows?
flashcards.a: Because reflection adds an extra processing step that slows down the system, so you need to prove it meaningfully improves performance.

flashcards.q: What is the main issue with asking an LLM to directly compare two outputs?
flashcards.a: LLMs often suffer from position bias, meaning they tend to prefer whichever option is presented first.

flashcards.q: How can you get more consistent results when using an LLM to judge subjective tasks?
flashcards.a: By grading against a set of binary criteria and summing the scores rather than asking for a single open-ended score.

notes.importance_reason: It explains how adding external feedback overcomes the performance limits of standard prompt engineering and internal reflection.
notes.tldr: Using external feedback in agent reflection helps bypass the performance plateaus of basic prompt engineering.
notes.summary: When building AI applications, direct prompt engineering eventually hits a performance plateau where further tuning stops helping. Adding reflection helps, but relying solely on a language model to reflect on its own output limits how much new information it can consider. By introducing external feedback—such as code execution results, regex pattern matching, web searches, or programmatic word counts—you provide genuinely new facts for the language model to use. This external input drives performance well past the typical plateau.

key_ideas.detail: Over time, tuning prompts yields diminishing returns and performance flattens out.
An LM reflecting on its own previous output uses no new information, whereas external feedback brings in fresh facts.
Simple software tools like regex matchers, web searches, and word counters can automatically generate helpful criticisms for the LM.

example.title: Fixing Word Limits with a Tool
example.scenario: An LM writes copy for a blog post or research abstract, but it frequently exceeds the strict word limit because LMs struggle with exact counts.
steps: The LM generates a draft of the text.
A simple word count tool programmatically counts the exact number of words.
The tool identifies that the draft exceeds the maximum word limit.
This exact word count is fed back to the LM as criticism.
The LM uses the new feedback to rewrite the text and hit the desired length.
example.takeaway: Using a programmatic tool to check output constraints provides precise feedback that helps the LM fix its own mistakes.

watch.why: Shows the performance curve chart comparing zero-shot prompting, reflection, and external feedback.
Illustrates how code execution output and error messages act as feedback.

terms.definition: New information gathered from outside sources or tools that helps an AI evaluate and improve its work.
Directly generating an output from a language model using a prompt without prior examples or iterative tuning.

flashcards.q: Why does standard prompt engineering eventually stop improving performance?
flashcards.a: It hits a performance plateau where further prompt adjustments yield diminishing returns.

flashcards.q: What is the main limitation of using an LM as the only source of reflection?
flashcards.a: The LM only reflects on the same information it already had, without gaining new external facts.

notes.importance_reason: This lesson introduces the core concept of tool use, which is foundational for building advanced agentic AI applications.
notes.tldr: Tool use allows an LLM to decide when to request a function call to gather information or take actions.
notes.summary: LLMs on their own lack real-time data or specialized calculation abilities, but giving them access to tools bridges this gap. A tool is simply a function provided to the LLM that it can choose to invoke when prompted by a user query. The LLM evaluates the prompt, decides whether a tool is needed, requests the function call, receives the returned data, and then generates a final answer. Developers can provide a single tool or multiple tools, leaving the choice entirely up to the LLM.

key_ideas.detail: Tools are functions provided to an LLM that the model can request to call to take actions or gather information.
Unlike hard-coded developer workflows, the LLM autonomously decides whether it needs to use a tool based on the user prompt.
The workflow follows a sequence: user prompt, LLM tool request, function execution, result fed back to the LLM, and final output.
Developers can provide several tools at once, allowing the LLM to select the right one or even chain multiple tools together.

example.title: Checking the Current Time
example.scenario: A user asks an LLM what time it is right now, but the pre-trained model does not know the current time.
steps: The user prompts the LLM with the question: What time is it right now?
The LLM examines its available tools and decides to call the getCurrentTime function.
The function executes and returns the current time value.
The returned time is fed back into the LLM conversation history.
The LLM generates the final response stating the exact current time.
example.takeaway: Giving an LLM access to a specific function lets it answer questions it otherwise could not handle alone.

watch.why: The speaker illustrates the step-by-step sequence of how an input prompt interacts with tools and the LLM.
Shows the dashed box notation used on slides to represent a set of tools available to the LLM.

terms.definition: The capability of letting an LLM decide when to request a function call to take an action or gather information.
A block of code provided as a tool that an LLM can request to execute to solve specific tasks.

flashcards.q: Who decides whether a tool is called in an LLM application?
flashcards.a: The LLM itself decides whether or not to invoke a tool based on the user prompt.

flashcards.q: What happens after a tool function returns its value?
flashcards.a: The returned value is fed back into the LLM conversational history so it can generate the final answer.

notes.importance_reason: It explains the fundamental mechanics of how LLMs interact with external functions through text generation and developer code.
notes.tldr: LLMs do not call functions directly; instead, they output specific text requests that developers catch, execute, and feed back into the model.
notes.summary: This lesson walks through the step-by-step process of how an LLM triggers a tool. Because an LLM only generates text, it must output a specific formatted tag like FUNCTION to request a tool call. Developer-written code parses this output, executes the actual function, and feeds the result back into the conversational history. The LLM then uses that returned data to generate a final response to the user. Although modern LLMs use built-in native syntax instead of custom prompts, understanding this underlying loop is essential for agentic workflows.

key_ideas.idea: LLMs generate text, not function calls
key_ideas.detail: An LLM cannot execute code directly; it only knows how to generate output tokens.

key_ideas.idea: The LLM requests a tool via text
key_ideas.detail: By using prompts, you instruct the LLM to output a specific format like FUNCTION: getCurrentTime when it needs data.
Your custom code must parse the LLM output, call the actual function, and handle any required arguments like time zones.
The output of the executed function is fed back into the chat history so the LLM can read it and formulate a final answer.

example.title: Getting the current time in New Zealand
example.scenario: A user asks for the time in New Zealand, requiring the LLM to use a custom time function with an argument.
steps: User asks what time it is in New Zealand.
LLM reads the prompt instructions and outputs FUNCTION: getCurrentTime/Auckland.
Developer code detects the text, extracts the Auckland argument, and runs the actual getCurrentTime function.
The function returns 4 a.m., and developer code feeds this result back into the LLM conversation history.
LLM reads the 4 a.m. result and generates the final reply: It is 4 a.m. in New Zealand.
example.takeaway: The LLM triggers a tool by writing formatted text, leaving the execution and data-feeding steps to the developer's code.

nodes.label: User Asks Question
nodes.note: User wants to know the time

watch.why: Introduction explaining why LLM tool use might initially seem mysterious.
Overview of how prompting was used historically before native tool training.

terms.definition: A piece of code or function that an LLM can request to be executed to retrieve extra data or perform actions.
The log of user prompts, LLM outputs, and function results passed back and forth to maintain context.
An input value passed to a function, such as a specific time zone for a clock tool.

flashcards.q: Do LLMs execute functions directly?
flashcards.a: No, LLMs only generate text. They output a specific text format requesting a tool call, which developer code then executes.

flashcards.q: What happens after the developer code runs the requested tool function?
flashcards.a: The output of the function is fed back into the LLM's conversational history so it can generate a final response.

notes.importance_reason: This lesson explains the code syntax needed to give an LLM access to tools, which is fundamental for building agentic workflows.
notes.tldr: You can use the AISuite library to easily pass functions as tools to an LLM, which automatically reads your docstrings to describe those functions.
notes.summary: Writing code for tool use involves passing available tools into an LLM chat completion call. Libraries like AISuite simplify this by automatically turning Python docstrings into the JSON schemas that LLMs need to understand the tools. Some implementations require manual JSON schema creation and manual handling of tool execution, but AISuite handles these steps for you. It also uses a max turns parameter to prevent infinite loops of tool calling. Code execution is noted as a particularly powerful tool to give an LLM.

key_ideas.detail: The LLM does not technically execute the tool itself; it requests that you call the tool, though developers often say the LLM calls the tool for short.
Libraries like AISuite inspect Python function docstrings and comments to automatically create the JSON schema that describes the function to the LLM.
A ceiling called max turns is set on how many times an LLM can request one tool after another to prevent infinite loops.

key_ideas.idea: Code execution as a special tool
key_ideas.detail: Giving an LLM the ability to write code and having a tool execute it is an incredibly powerful capability.

example.title: Using AISuite to Give an LLM a Tool
example.scenario: You want an LLM to answer a time-related question by accessing a local function.
steps: Define a Python function like getCurrentTime with a clear docstring explaining what it does.
Write a chat completion call using the AISuite library, specifying model GPT-4o and passing your function into the tools parameter.
Let AISuite automatically convert your function name, description, and parameters into a JSON schema behind the scenes.
Execute the call, allowing the library to handle any tool requests and return the final response.
example.takeaway: Using a library like AISuite spares you from writing manual JSON schemas and lets the LLM understand your functions directly through Python docstrings.

watch.why: The instructor introduces the concept of tool calling versus tool requests.
A side-by-side view shows how a Python function's docstring becomes a JSON schema.

terms.definition: An open source Python package that makes it easy to call multiple LLM providers and automatically generates JSON schemas for tools.
A structured format used to describe a function's name, description, and parameters so an LLM knows how to use it.
A safety parameter that limits the maximum number of consecutive tool requests an LLM can make to prevent infinite loops.
A string literal in Python used to document a function, which AISuite reads to describe tools to the LLM.

flashcards.q: What does AISuite use to automatically generate a JSON schema for a Python function?
flashcards.a: It looks at the function's docstring and comments.

flashcards.q: Why is the max turns parameter included in tool-calling code?
flashcards.a: To stop the LLM from entering a potential infinite loop of calling one tool after another.

notes.importance_reason: It introduces code execution as a powerful alternative to building individual tools, which is a core concept in agentic AI.
notes.tldr: Allowing language models to write and execute code solves complex tasks like math problems without needing a separate tool for every function.
notes.summary: Instead of creating a new tool for every math operation like square roots or exponents, you can prompt a language model to write code that solves the user's query. You extract this code using tags, run it using a tool like Python's exec function or a sandbox, and pass the numerical answer back to the model. If the code fails, you can pass the error message back to let the model reflect and fix its mistake. Because running arbitrary code carries security risks such as deleting files, using a safe sandbox environment is a best practice.

key_ideas.idea: Code execution replaces many single-purpose tools
key_ideas.detail: Instead of building separate tools for every calculation button, letting the model write code handles complex and varied math tasks easily.
You prompt the model to return code wrapped in specific tags, use regular expressions to extract it, and execute it to get the result.
If the generated code fails, passing the error message back to the model allows it to revise the code and try again.
Executing arbitrary code can lead to accidental data loss or file deletion, so running code inside a secure sandbox like Docker or E2B is a best practice.

example.title: Solving a Square Root Query
example.scenario: A user asks an application to calculate the square root of two.
steps: The language model is prompted to write code to solve the query and wrap it in execute Python tags.
The model generates Python code calculating the square root.
The application uses regular expressions to extract the code between the tags.
The application executes the code and obtains the numerical answer.
The model formats the numerical answer into a final response for the user.
example.takeaway: Allowing the model to write and execute code enables it to solve math queries without requiring a dedicated square root tool.

watch.why: Visual example of extracting code from tags.

terms.definition: Allowing a language model to write and run computer code to solve tasks.
A built-in Python function that executes code passed to it as a string.
A secure, isolated environment used to safely run untrusted code without risking system damage.

flashcards.q: Why is code execution preferred over building individual math tools?
flashcards.a: It avoids needing a separate tool for every possible calculator function or math operation.

flashcards.q: What is a best practice to prevent generated code from damaging your system?
flashcards.a: Running the code inside a safe sandbox environment like Docker or E2B.

notes.importance_reason: MCP is a fundamental standard for connecting large language models to tools and data sources efficiently.
notes.tldr: Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how applications connect to tools and data, reducing custom integration work.
notes.summary: Instead of every application team writing custom wrappers for every tool like Slack, GitHub, or databases, MCP provides a standard protocol. This changes integration work from multiplying applications by tools to simply adding them together. MCP uses a client-server architecture where clients are the applications consuming tools and servers provide access to the tools and data. Using an MCP client, a user can easily fetch files, check pull requests, and let the LLM generate a summary.

key_ideas.detail: Without a standard, M applications needing N tools require M times N custom wrappers, which MCP reduces to M plus N.
MCP provides access to both static data fetching (resources) and general executable functions.
MCP clients are the applications consuming tools, while MCP servers are the software wrappers providing data and actions.

example.title: Summarizing a GitHub repository
example.scenario: A cloud desktop app connected to a GitHub MCP server wants to fetch and summarize a repository's readme file.
steps: User enters a query asking to summarize the readme markdown file from a specific GitHub repository.
The application acts as an MCP client and uses the GitHub MCP server to request the file.
The MCP server retrieves the file content and feeds it back to the LLM's context.
The LLM generates a clear text summary of the markdown file for the user.
example.takeaway: An MCP client cleanly communicates with an MCP server to fetch external data and feed it to the LLM.

watch.why: Explanation of how MCP simplifies integration work from M times N to M plus N.

terms.definition: A standard proposed by Anthropic that gives an LLM access to more context and tools.
An application that wants access to external tools or data sources.
A software wrapper that provides access to data and actions from sources like Slack, GitHub, or Google Drive.
MCP tools focused specifically on fetching data.

flashcards.q: What major integration pain point does MCP solve?
flashcards.a: It reduces custom integration work from M times N to M plus N by creating a single standard.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between an MCP client and an MCP server?
flashcards.a: The client is the application consuming the tools, while the server is the software wrapper providing access to data and actions.

lessons.title: Evaluations (evals)
lessons.module: Module 4 - Practical Tips for Building Agentic AI

notes.importance_reason: This lesson teaches how to build evaluations to track progress and guide improvements in agentic AI systems.
notes.tldr: Build a quick prototype, inspect its outputs to find errors, and create targeted evaluations to track system improvements.
notes.summary: When building agentic AI, it is best to quickly build a prototype and review its outputs to discover where it fails. For example, invoice extraction might struggle with due dates, or a copy assistant might write text that is too long. Once you identify a specific error mode, you can build an evaluation set with 10 to 20 examples to track your progress. Evals can range from objective code checks to subjective LLM-as-a-judge scoring, with or without per-example ground truth. Over time, you can expand and refine your eval set so that it better matches your human judgment.

key_ideas.detail: Avoid spending weeks theorizing; build a quick system responsibly so you can look at its actual outputs and find errors.
Collect 10 to 20 test inputs to measure specific failure modes, such as incorrect date extraction or overly long text.
Evals vary by how outputs are measured (code or LLM-as-a-judge) and whether they use a per-example ground truth.
Just as your system improves, your eval set should grow and adapt over time to better reflect your personal judgment.

example.title: Invoice Due Date Evaluation
example.scenario: An invoice processing workflow extracts four required fields, but testing reveals it frequently mixes up the issue date with the due date.
steps: Collect 10 to 20 sample invoices and manually record the correct due dates as ground truth.
Instruct the LLM via prompt to format all extracted due dates in a standard year-month-date format.
Write Python code using regular expressions to extract the date from the LLM output.
Compare the extracted date to the ground truth annotation to calculate an accuracy percentage.
example.takeaway: Using a small evaluation set allows you to test prompt adjustments and measure whether due date extraction accuracy goes up.

terms.definition: An evaluation used to measure the accuracy or performance of an AI system.
The verified correct answer or label manually created for a test example.
Using a large language model to evaluate and score the output of another system.
An evaluation that tests the performance of the entire system from user prompt to final output.

flashcards.q: Why is it recommended to build a quick prototype before designing evals?
flashcards.a: Looking at initial outputs helps you discover where the system actually fails so you know what to evaluate.

flashcards.q: What are the two main axes used to categorize end-to-end evaluations?
flashcards.a: How outputs are evaluated (code vs. LLM judge) and whether there is a per-example ground truth.

lessons.title: Error analysis and prioritizing next steps
lessons.module: Module 4 - Practical Tips for Building Agentic AI

notes.importance_reason: It teaches a disciplined method to find where agentic workflows fail so you do not waste months guessing.
notes.tldr: Use error analysis and intermediate traces to find which step causes system failures and prioritize your fixes.
notes.summary: When an agentic workflow does not work as well as you want, guessing where to fix it can waste months of work. Instead, you should examine the intermediate outputs of each step, known as the trace, to spot which component is performing poorly. Focusing on examples where the system made an error allows you to build a spreadsheet and count up where the mistakes happen most often. By combining these error frequencies with your ideas for improvement, you can decide which component to prioritize. This disciplined approach ensures you spend your time on changes that actually improve the overall system.

key_ideas.detail: Look at the intermediate output after each step in a workflow to understand how each component performs.
Set aside satisfactory runs and concentrate your error analysis entirely on cases where the final output is not satisfactory.

key_ideas.idea: Use a spreadsheet to count errors
key_ideas.detail: Build a spreadsheet to explicitly track and count which components perform significantly worse than a human expert would.

key_ideas.idea: Prioritize based on frequency and ideas
key_ideas.detail: Choose to work on components that generate frequent errors and where you actually have a clear idea for improvement.

example.title: Error Analysis for a Research Agent
example.scenario: A research agent misses key points in essays, and you need to find out why.
steps: Gather a set of essay prompts where the research agent produced unsatisfactory outputs.
Inspect the intermediate outputs for each step, such as search terms and search results.
Record errors in a spreadsheet, noting whether search terms or search results failed to meet human expert standards.
Count the error frequencies to discover that search results fail 45% of the time while search terms only fail 5% of the time.
Prioritize fixing the web search engine or tuning its parameters since it causes the most frequent errors.
example.takeaway: Tracking component errors in a spreadsheet prevents you from guessing and shows you exactly where to focus your engineering efforts.

The output of a single step within a computer workflow.
The systematic process of examining system failures to determine which component is most responsible.

flashcards.a: The overall set of outputs produced by all the intermediate steps during a single run.

flashcards.q: Why should you use a spreadsheet during error analysis?
flashcards.a: To explicitly count up how often each component fails so you can prioritize your work.

flashcards.q: What two factors should guide your choice of what component to fix?
flashcards.a: The frequency of errors in that component and whether you have practical ideas for improving it.

lessons.title: More error analysis examples

notes.importance_reason: It provides practical walkthroughs of error analysis on two realistic workflows to help developers build intuition.
notes.tldr: Practical examples show how error analysis helps identify which workflow component causes the most failures.
notes.summary: This lesson walks through two examples of error analysis for agentic workflows: invoice processing and customer email response. For invoice processing, looking at subpar examples reveals whether PDF-to-text conversion or large language model extraction is at fault. For customer emails, checking unsatisfactory outputs helps determine if the issue lies in the database query, the database data, or the final draft. Categorizing these errors in a spreadsheet prevents wasting weeks tuning the wrong part of the system.

key_ideas.detail: Ignore the inputs that the system handled correctly and analyze between 10 and 100 failing examples.
Go through a handful of failing cases and tally which component was responsible for each error.
Error analysis stops teams from spending weeks tuning a component that is not actually causing the main problems.
Percentages in an error analysis may not add up to 100% because multiple components can fail on a single example.

example.scenario: An agentic workflow processes customer order emails by querying a database and drafting a response.
steps: Gather a batch of emails where the final output was unsatisfactory.
Review each failing email to see what went wrong in the pipeline.
Check whether the LM wrote an incorrect database query, the database had bad data, or the final email draft was poor.
Tally up the causes to find that 75 percent of errors stem from incorrect database queries.
Focus improvement efforts on fixing how the LM writes queries rather than fixing other parts.
example.takeaway: Quantifying the source of errors guides you directly to the component that needs the most attention.

flashcards.a: Because looking at subpar performance helps you figure out what went wrong.

lessons.title: Component-level evaluations
lessons.module: Module 4 - Practical Tips for Building Agentic AI

notes.importance_reason: It teaches how to isolate and evaluate single agent components to test improvements efficiently.
notes.tldr: Evaluate individual agent components separately to test changes faster and avoid system noise.
notes.summary: Rerunning an entire agent workflow for every small change is expensive and hides improvements behind system noise. Instead, component-level evaluations test single parts, like a web search tool, by comparing outputs to expert-approved gold standards. This allows developers to tune hyperparameters and swap search engines efficiently. Once the component is optimized, you can run an end-to-end evaluation to check overall performance. This targeted approach helps teams isolate errors and work much faster.

key_ideas.detail: Running the full agent workflow for every change is slow and makes it hard to spot small improvements due to system randomness.
Experts create a list of authoritative web pages for specific queries to serve as the correct answer benchmark.
Evaluating just one part lets you quickly test different search engines, parameters, or result counts.
Component metrics give teams a direct way to measure progress without worrying about the rest of the complex system.

example.title: Evaluating a Research Agent Web Search Component
example.scenario: You want to improve the web search quality for a research agent without running the full agent workflow every time.
steps: Gather a small set of test queries for the search component.
Ask an expert to define gold standard web resources for each query.
Write code to compare the web search results against the gold standard list using standard retrieval metrics.
Test different search engines or parameters to see which setup has higher overlap with the gold standard.
example.takeaway: You can quickly find the best search configuration without waiting on the slow, noisy end-to-end agent workflow.

terms.definition: An evaluation focused on measuring the performance of a single part of an agent system rather than the whole workflow.
A curated list of authoritative web pages determined by experts to be the best answers for specific search queries.
An evaluation that tests the entire agent workflow from start to finish.

flashcards.q: Why might you avoid using only end-to-end evaluations when tuning a component?
flashcards.a: Because they are expensive to run and system noise makes it hard to see small improvements in a single component.

flashcards.a: An expert-approved list of authoritative web pages that a search query should ideally find.

notes.importance_reason: It teaches practical techniques for benchmarking and optimizing the latency and cost of agentic workflows.
notes.tldr: Focus on output quality first, then use step-by-step benchmarking to optimize latency and cost when needed.
notes.summary: When building agentic workflows, prioritize high output quality before worrying about cost and latency. Once optimization becomes necessary, start by timing each step in the workflow to identify bottlenecks. You can reduce latency by using parallelism or switching to smaller models and faster providers. Similarly, calculate the cost of each individual step to find where you can swap in cheaper components or models. Benchmarking ensures you focus your efforts on the parts of the workflow that actually matter.

key_ideas.detail: Focus on getting high-quality outputs first, and worry about cost and latency only after the workflow is working well.
Time each component of your workflow to see which specific steps take the longest and have the most room for improvement.
Reduce latency by running independent operations at the same time or by testing smaller, faster language models and providers.
Calculate the expense of each token, API call, and computational step to locate the biggest financial contributors.

lessons.title: Planning workflows

notes.importance_reason: This lesson introduces the planning design pattern, which is a core concept for building autonomous agents that choose their own tool sequences.
notes.tldr: An LLM can write a step-by-step plan using available tools, and then execute each step in turn to handle complex user requests.
notes.summary: Instead of hard-coding a fixed sequence of steps, you give a large language model a list of tools and ask it to output a plan. The agent then executes each step of the plan one by one, passing the output of one step into the context of the next. This flexible approach allows the agent to handle diverse tasks like searching inventory or managing emails. While widely used in autonomous coding systems, planning can be harder to control because the exact runtime steps are dynamic. Future videos will dive deeper into how these execution steps are strung together.

key_ideas.detail: Autonomous agents use the planning pattern to decide their own steps instead of relying on hard-coded sequences.
You give the LLM a set of tools with clear descriptions so it knows what capabilities it can use in its plan.
Once the LLM writes a multi-step plan, you task the LLM to carry out each step sequentially, feeding previous outputs forward.
Planning can make systems harder to control because developers do not know in advance what runtime plan the LLM will generate.

example.takeaway: The agent dynamically figures out the correct combination and order of tools without a pre-written program.

lessons.title: Creating and executing LLM plans

notes.importance_reason: This lesson teaches how to format and parse LLM-generated plans using structured data formats like JSON, which is essential for autonomous agent workflows.
notes.tldr: Instructing an LLM to output plans in JSON or XML allows downstream code to parse and execute steps reliably.
notes.summary: To move beyond simple text descriptions, developers prompt LLMs to format their execution plans in structured formats like JSON or XML. By defining a clear format with keys and values for descriptions, tools, and arguments, downstream code can easily read and execute each step. While XML is also popular, JSON is widely supported and prevents the ambiguity found in markdown or plain text. This structured approach lets workflows execute agent plans systematically one step at a time.

key_ideas.detail: Developers ask LLMs to format plans in structured ways rather than plain English to make them machine-readable.
JSON is a preferred format because leading LLMs generate it well and downstream code can clearly parse steps, tools, and arguments.
XML with delimiters and tags is another reliable option for structuring plan steps, while markdown and plain text are more ambiguous.
Once a plan is parsed from a structured format like JSON, workflows can reliably execute the steps one by one.

lessons.title: Planning with code execution
lessons.module: Module 5 - Patterns for Highly Autonomous Agents

notes.importance_reason: It introduces code execution as a powerful alternative to traditional tool use and JSON plans for agentic workflows.
notes.tldr: Instead of using custom tools or JSON formats, letting a language model write and execute code allows it to create flexible, multi-step plans.
notes.summary: Asking a language model to output a plan step-by-step in JSON or giving it dozens of narrow custom tools can become brittle and inefficient. By having the model write code using standard data processing libraries like pandas, it gains access to thousands of built-in functions. The model can string together complex operations to answer queries about datasets. Research shows that code as an action outperforms plain text and JSON plans across many models. Developers must still remember to run generated code in a safe sandbox environment.

key_ideas.detail: Creating a new tool for every possible user query leads to a brittle, inefficient system with too many edge cases.
Prompting the language model to write code lets it use massive existing libraries like pandas instead of relying on custom tools.
Studies show that code as an action yields superior performance compared to text or JSON-based plans.
Highly agentic software assistants use detailed plans and checklists to build and test complex software components step by step.

notes.tldr: Complex tasks can be broken down into multi-agent systems where different AI agents take on specific roles like researchers or writers.
notes.summary: A multi-agent workflow involves multiple AI agents collaborating to complete a complex task, much like a human team with different roles. Developers can build individual agents by prompting a large language model to play a specific part, such as a researcher, graphic designer, or writer, and equipping them with relevant tools. These agents can then be organized in a simple linear sequence or coordinated dynamically by a manager agent. This approach helps decompose difficult tasks into manageable subtasks and allows for better focus and potential reuse of individual agents.

key_ideas.detail: Complex tasks can be divided among specialized roles, such as researchers, graphic designers, and writers, mirroring human teams.
Different agents need different tools, like web search for researchers or image generation and code execution for graphic designers.
Individual agents are created by prompting a large language model to play a specific role with distinct instructions and capabilities.
Agents can work together in a straight linear sequence or be coordinated by a manager agent that delegates and oversees tasks.

lessons.title: Communication patterns for multi-agent systems

notes.importance_reason: It introduces the fundamental communication patterns used to structure multi-agent systems.
notes.tldr: Multi-agent systems use various communication patterns, ranging from simple linear flows to hierarchical structures and open-ended networks.
notes.summary: Designing communication patterns for multi-agent systems is complex, similar to organizing human teams. The two most common patterns are linear plans and one-level hierarchies managed by a central coordinator. More advanced setups include deeper hierarchies where agents manage sub-agents, and all-to-all networks where anyone can talk to anyone. While simpler patterns offer control, all-to-all communication introduces unpredictability and chaos. Software frameworks are available to help developers easily implement these different communication styles.

key_ideas.detail: Agents work in a sequence where the output of one agent passes to the next, such as a researcher passing to a designer then a writer.
A central manager agent coordinates the work by sending tasks to and collecting results from various team members.
A more advanced structure where manager agents oversee team members who themselves call on smaller sub-agents like fact checkers.
An experimental setup where every agent can talk to any other agent at any time, which creates unpredictable results.

example.takeaway: Structuring how agents pass messages dictates the predictability and control of the final multi-agent output.
